# Block 2: Debugging with AI {.unnumbered} AI is a fast debugging partner for code you wrote yourself, because you can judge its answer against what you meant. You fix two bugs that raise no error: one the data reveal, and one that only your knowledge of the study catches. *⏱ ~20 minutes · Start on `main`, Git pane clean, Claude Code running in Manual mode.* :::{#block2-files .callout-note collapse="true"} ## This block's files, and how it fits The first live block in your workshop repository ([setup](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#your-workshop-repository)). The code you fix is practice, so it goes in the git-ignored `scratch/` folder; there is no checkpoint branch, because nothing later depends on it. A misspelt function name, a bug the AI can fix alone, is in *Going further*. | File | Where it comes from | Used in | |---|---|---| | `data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv` | Shipped with the template: 72 voles, 24 per treatment arm | Both exercises | | `AGENTS.md` | Shipped with the template; Claude Code reads it at the start of every conversation | Exercise 1, step 3: the line you did not ask for | | `scratch/debugging.R` | You create it, in Exercise 1, step 1 | Both exercises | ::: ## Exercise 1: A logic error :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} A logic error (12 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **Goal:** find a bug that raises no error by inspecting the data first, so that you can check the agent's diagnosis against evidence you have seen yourself. **Start state:** your workshop repository on `main`; Claude Code in Manual mode, with a new conversation (`/clear`). :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Using another tool **Posit Assistant:** type `/ask` first. Ask mode is read-only: it cannot edit files or run R code, so the answer-only line is not needed. It does see the names and types of the objects in your session (not their values) and can read your console history, so it may already have your `distinct()` output: that is a disclosure route too ([Block 3](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd)). For step 4, type `/normal` so it can run the diagnostics in your live R session, approving each call; `/normal` is also how you leave Ask mode. **A chat window:** paste the same prompts, without the answer-only line, and skip step 4. ::: **1. Set up.** In the R console, `usethis::edit_file("scratch/debugging.R")` creates this block's practice script and opens it. Paste this in and run it; the last two commands are code you wrote to compute mean post-treatment mass for high-dose voles: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(here) voles <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv")) high_dose <- voles |> filter(treatment_arm == "high_dose") high_dose |> summarise(mean_mass = mean(mass_post_g)) ``` ::: It runs without error but returns `NaN`: the bug is in what you asked for, so put the evidence in front of you first, then in front of the assistantAny AI tool that helps you write or understand code, from inline completion to a chat window. In this course “assistant” is the general word; “agent” is used when the tool acts on your files.. **2. Inspect the data before asking for help.** In the R console: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} voles |> distinct(treatment_arm) voles |> count(treatment_arm) nrow(high_dose) ``` ::: The values are `Control`, `Low_dose` and `High_dose`, and `nrow()` is zero: you have found the bug yourself in seconds. **3. Ask with the evidence in hand.** Paste the code and the diagnostic output together, so that the answer rests on the real values, not a guess. **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text I am trying to compute mean post-treatment mass for high-dose voles. My code: high_dose <- voles |> filter(treatment_arm == "high_dose") high_dose |> summarise(mean_mass = mean(mass_post_g)) returns NaN. But voles |> distinct(treatment_arm) returns "Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose". I think the filter fails because of the capitalisation. Is that the only problem? Answer from what I've pasted: don't read files, run code or edit anything. ``` If it asks to run a command or edit a file despite the last line, choose **No**. **Answer each request with plain Yes or No.** Never choose an option that says *don't ask again*: it saves a rule that skips the question from then on. Ignore a first line `# agents-md: active v1` in its code: [Block 4](11e-instructions-skills.qmd) explains it. :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## How it works: asking an agent only to answer Claude Code is an agentAn assistant that can read across a project’s files and, depending on its permission mode, edit them and run commands, such as Claude Code. An agent acts; a chat window only advises.: given a question, it may search your project, read files and offer to run code. The answer-only line is only a request: Claude Code has no ask mode, and plan mode is not used here because it still reads your files while it plans. Manual mode is the control: it must ask before it runs a command or edits a file, and your answer decides. Claude Code cannot see the objects in your R console, such as `voles`: it sees your data only by reading files or running code, and each `Rscript` command it runs starts a fresh R process. Check its work in the R console ([checking work](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#checking-work)). ::: **4. Now let the agent gather the evidence.** This is the one step in the block where it acts. Type `/clear`, so that it starts without the evidence you pasted, then: **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text Read data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv and run R code with Rscript to find why filtering treatment_arm for "high_dose" returns no rows. Don't edit any files. Show each command and its output. ``` It reads the file without asking (reading needs no approval), but asks before it runs R. Approve a run only if you can say what it does and why you want it now; refusing is always safe. Here you can, so choose **Yes** if the `Rscript` command only reads the data and prints results. Then compare its diagnosis with yours from step 2. **Keep this conversation open:** in Block 3 you read its transcript to see what reached the model provider.
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} high_dose <- voles |> filter(treatment_arm == "High_dose") high_dose |> summarise(mean_mass = mean(mass_post_g, na.rm = TRUE)) ``` ::: The filter now matches the data. `na.rm = TRUE` is a precaution for real data, which usually have missing values.
**You are done when** `nrow(high_dose)` is 24, the mean is a number, not `NaN`, and the agent's diagnosis in step 4 matches yours from step 2. **If it goes wrong:** if `nrow()` is still zero, run `voles |> distinct(treatment_arm)` again and copy the value exactly as printed. :::: ::: ## Exercise 2: A correct-looking but wrong result :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} A correct-looking but wrong result (8 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **Goal:** catch a result that runs cleanly but is wrong by stating the expected answer before you ask, so that a plausible but wrong number does not reach your results. **Start state:** `scratch/debugging.R` is open with `voles` loaded. Ask in Exercise 1's conversation, without `/clear`, so that its transcript is still there for Block 3. You wrote this to get the mean change in body mass by treatment arm. Paste it into `scratch/debugging.R` and run it: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} voles |> mutate(mass_change_g = mass_pre_g - mass_post_g) |> summarise(mean_change = mean(mass_change_g), .by = treatment_arm) ``` ::: It runs, and the numbers look plausible. But the treatment was designed to increase mass, and they say mass falls. Only your knowledge of the study reveals the error: an AI catches it only if you tell it what the answer should be. **1. Write down what a correct result should look like, then compare.** Here: positive values, rising from Control to High_dose. The mismatch is the diagnosis. **2. Ask for a second opinion, stating the expected direction.** **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text This should show mass gain increasing with dose, but the values are negative and decreasing. What is wrong? voles |> mutate(mass_change_g = mass_pre_g - mass_post_g) |> summarise(mean_change = mean(mass_change_g), .by = treatment_arm) Answer from what I've pasted: don't read files, run code or edit anything. ```
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} voles |> mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post_g - mass_pre_g) |> summarise(mean_change = mean(mass_change_g), .by = treatment_arm) ``` ::: `mass_change_g` is post minus pre: gain, not loss. The original ran without complaint because subtraction works in either direction.
**You are done when** your corrected means are positive and increase from Control to High_dose, as you predicted in step 1. **If it goes wrong:** if the values are still negative, check which mass you subtract from which: post minus pre is gain. :::: ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The debugging checklist Inspect the data first, ask the AI second. 1. **Read the error in full:** the function name and the phrase usually locate the bug. 2. **Inspect the data:** `glimpse()`, `distinct()`, `summary()`, and `nrow()` after a filter. 3. **Check names exactly,** including capitals and underscores. 4. **Then ask,** giving the code, the error and the diagnostic output together. Ask for an answer, not an action, until you have the evidence. 5. **Explain the fix in one sentence** before you accept it. 6. **Before trusting a clean run,** state what the result should look like (sign, size, order) and compare. ::: :::{.callout-note} ## Check · Reproduce · Record - **You can now:** use an assistant to diagnose and fix errors in your own code, **trusted because** you inspect the data first and explain each fix in a sentence. - **Check:** before trusting a clean run, state the sign and size the result should have, and compare. - **Reproduce:** rerun the fixed code in a fresh R sessionAn R session with nothing loaded from earlier work: Session > Restart R in RStudio or Positron (with “never save .RData” set, as on Day 1), callr::rscript() from the console, or Rscript in the terminal. Code that only works in your current session depends on something you did not record., so it does not depend on a leftover object. - **Record:** nothing to log yet; the AI-use log starts in [Block 3](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd). ::: ## Check your understanding **A filter returns zero rows and the summary is `NaN`, with no error. What should you do before asking an AI?**
**Code runs without error and returns plausible numbers. What is the most reliable first check?**
## Going further (not covered live) This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you. :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## A misspelt function name (self-study) **Goal:** fix an error with Claude Code's help and explain the fix in one sentence, so that you accept only a fix you understand. **Start state:** `scratch/debugging.R` is open with `voles` loaded, and Claude Code has a new conversation (`/clear`). During the workshop, wait until after Block 3, which reads Exercise 1's conversation. You wrote this in `scratch/debugging.R` to count voles per treatment: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(voles, aes(x = treatment_arm)) + geom_barchart() ``` ::: R returns: ``` Error in geom_barchart(): could not find function "geom_barchart" ``` **1. Ask for a fix.** Paste the code and the error, and ask. **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text This code gives an error: ggplot(voles, aes(x = treatment_arm)) + geom_barchart() Error in geom_barchart(): could not find function "geom_barchart" What is wrong, and what is the fix? Answer from what I've pasted: don't read files, run code or edit anything. ``` **2. Explain it before you accept it.** Write one sentence saying why the original failed. If you can write it, you understood the fix; that sentence is your check.
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(voles, aes(x = treatment_arm)) + geom_bar() ``` ::: The function is `geom_bar()`; ggplot2's geoms have no `_chart` suffix. This is not a syntax error: R parses the code without complaint, and fails only when it looks for a function called `geom_barchart()` and finds none. "Could not find function" means no loaded package has a function of that name.
**You are done when** the corrected plot draws a bar for each treatment arm, and you have written your one-sentence explanation. **If it goes wrong:** if the fix produces a different error, paste that error back in the same conversation; the assistant now has two clues. ::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## An aesthetic-mapping error This error needs ggplot2's grammar rather than the data. You wanted a scatter plot of post-treatment metabolic rate against post-treatment mass, coloured by treatment arm: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(voles, aes(x = mass_post_g, y = metabolic_rate_post)) + geom_point(color = treatment_arm) + labs(title = "Metabolic rate by mass") ``` ::: R returns an error saying that object `treatment_arm` was not found. The exact wording varies between ggplot2 versions. **1. Ask for a fix.** Before accepting it, write one sentence on why ggplot2 could not find `treatment_arm`.
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(voles, aes(x = mass_post_g, y = metabolic_rate_post)) + geom_point(aes(colour = treatment_arm)) + labs(title = "Metabolic rate by mass") ``` ::: `treatment_arm` is a column in the data, so the mapping must go inside `aes()`. An argument outside `aes()`, such as `color =`, expects a fixed value like `"red"` or `"#0072B2"`. ggplot2 looked for an object called `treatment_arm` in your environment, found none, and stopped. `colour` and `color` are interchangeable in ggplot2.
